bull_bear.body:
- NARCL residual ₹380 cr (vs ₹700 cr agreed), prepaying ahead of schedule; minimum ₹45 cr more in FY27 to neutralize FY27-28 liability; then attack FY28-29.
- Deleveraging funded ~entirely by arbitration award monetization (~75% of proceeds → NARCL), NOT operating cash flow → operating surplus freed for growth (BESS capex, WC).
- Equity raised ₹476 cr (promoter-heavy) demonstrates skin-in-the-game; bank limit ₹505 cr; surety bonds ₹305 cr to economize on BG/margin.
- No dividend discussed. Tax shield: accumulated losses >₹500 cr + new tax regime (no MAT) → minimal cash tax for "a few years."
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation (deleveraging — central)

bull_bear.body:
- **Arbitration dependency:** Entire deleveraging thesis hinges on timely arbitration realizations (~40% claim-to-award conversion assumed; some at Supreme Court — timing/quantum uncertain).
- **Legacy NARCL dues** still ₹380 cr on books despite "effectively debt-free" framing.
- **Working capital / receivables:** receivables jumped to ₹417.5 cr; reliance on escrow/back-to-back netting; govt-payment cycle risk (esp. PHED/state water vs NTPC/PowerGrid which pay in 15–30 days).
- **Jal Jeevan payment risk:** mgmt acknowledges JJM payments were stopped for verification (now resuming); SPML avoided JJM during stress, only re-entering selectively.
- **Funding-paced execution:** revenue calibrated to customer fund availability → top-line lumpiness (FY26 miss); West-Asia-war crude/supply headwinds (mitigated by PV clauses).
- **BESS execution risk:** new manufacturing vertical, ambitious capacity ramp, oversupply concern (mgmt downplays via Energy Vault tie-up + 30-40 yr power EPC pedigree).
- **One-off-reliant Q4 PAT** (tax reversal + liability write-back) — quality of earnings.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident, detailed, candid on the FY26 turnover miss (owned it, explained funding discipline). Repeatedly stresses "SPML 2.0" discipline — quality over volume, ≥10% margin floor, PV clause, fully-funded orders only. CFO Manoj Digga dominated; technical BESS depth from Malay Chakraborti. Framing of "effectively debt-free" is optimistic and should be read against ₹380 cr residual NARCL + arbitration-timing risk. Promoter has injected meaningful equity — alignment positive.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The real deleveraging engine is the litigation book (~₹4,500 cr claims), not EBITDA — SPML is partly an arbitration-recovery story dressed as an EPC.
- "Order book met, turnover missed" — for an EPC the order book is the leading indicator; FY26 shortfall is a timing (funding-paced) issue that converts to FY27-28 revenue, not a demand loss.
- BESS is genuinely differentiated optionality (only Indian player with Energy Vault tie-up + own battery-pack/container manufacturing) but is capacity/execution unproven — a 5 GW line implies ~₹5,000 cr revenue potential vs ₹868 cr current total.
- Margin trajectory is structurally up purely on mix shift (legacy run-off → new ≥10% orders) even before BESS scales.
- Back-to-back legacy contracts inflate gross receivables/payables but are cash-flow-neutral — headline WC looks worse than economic reality.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Net worth grew from Rs 509 Cr (FY24) to Rs 819 Cr (FY25) to Rs 999 Cr (FY26); Debt-to-Equity declined from 1.1x (FY24) to 0.4x (FY26) and further to 0.34x (Jun-26); ROE improved from 4% (FY24) to 8% (FY26).
- Equity raised since 2022 via preferential allotment to fund growth in Water, Power and BESS plus capex/working capital; the deck states two different totals in different slides - Rs 819 Cr (promoters ~Rs 400 Cr) on the Preferential Allotment slide vs Rs 650 Cr (promoters Rs 388 Cr) on the Key Strengths slide.
- NARCL/IDRCL legacy debt: Rs 700 Cr settlement structured over 8 years, of which Rs 325 Cr already repaid and Rs 375 Cr outstanding, to be serviced from arbitration award proceeds (Rs 678 Cr in hand against Rs 4,526 Cr of claims filed, ~40% expected to convert to awards); no additional interest outgo anticipated.
- Credit profile strengthened: CRISIL assigned and ICRA upgraded rating to BBB (Stable); Rs 860 Cr credit facility enhancement from a PSU bank plus ~Rs 300 Cr surety bond drawl to support execution and bidding capacity.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Tender / order-inflow dependence on government schemes — MD&A states a material part of revenue depends on the pace and scale of tenders floated by Government/municipal bodies under schemes such as Jal Jeevan Mission and AMRUT 2.0. This is structural: BRSR records EPC and O&M for Central and State Government infrastructure as 100% of turnover, with exports at 0%, so there is no non-government or overseas revenue to offset a slowdown in domestic scheme tendering.
- Receivables and working-capital risk with government counterparties — EPC contracts with government counterparties carry inherent risk of delayed collections and retention money release, notwithstanding mitigation through escrow mechanisms. The Chairman's message reinforces this, noting the renewed water portfolio requires working capital as execution gathers pace and that liquidity and cash conversion remain central to decisions; BRSR reports accounts payable days of 272 in FY2025-26 (267 in FY2024-25), including retention money.
- Execution risk on project delivery — MD&A flags project delays arising from land acquisition, right-of-way, monsoon/seasonal factors and contractor/sub-contractor performance. The Chairman frames the same point commercially: an order is only the beginning of a commitment, and its real economics emerge through engineering, procurement, execution, billing and collection — the quality of the order book will be demonstrated through conversion.
- Financial and leverage risk tied to the NARCL settlement — Continued servicing of the NARCL settlement — a `700 crore total obligation over 8 years, of which `290 crore has been repaid — remains linked to the timing of awards-in-hand and expected recoveries on filed claims. MD&A separately states debt obligations of approximately `380 crore including interest over the next five years are expected to be met through arbitration proceeds of approximately `627 crore, so repayment capacity is contingent on recoveries the Company does not control.
- New-business risk in the BESS vertical — The BESS segment is at a relatively early stage for the Company, carrying technology, supply-chain and demand-ramp-up risk associated with the Energy Vault collaboration and the planned manufacturing facility in Maharashtra. The segment remains in build-out and is only expected to be operational from 2026-2027, while the licensed technology is not yet fully absorbed and certification milestones are still ahead.
- Regulatory and policy risk on scheme funding — Changes in government infrastructure policy, funding allocations (for example under JJM, AMRUT, or VGF for BESS) or energy storage obligation timelines could affect the pace of order inflow. MD&A separately flags that changes in environmental regulations, labour laws and other statutory requirements may increase compliance obligations and affect operational efficiency and cost structures.
- Litigation and contingent-liability exposure — MD&A flags ongoing legal and arbitration matters as disclosed elsewhere in the Annual Report and financial statements. This matters doubly because the Company also treats expected arbitration recoveries as the primary source of debt-repayment coverage, so adverse or delayed outcomes cut both ways.
- Execution pace tied to client-side fund availability, and commodity/geopolitical cost exposure — MD&A states business selection and billing pace are tied to project fund availability, and any tightening at the client or agency level could affect revenue-recognition timelines; it cites the West Asia conflict, elevated crude prices and supply disruptions as having constrained fund availability and execution pace in March FY26. Commodity and energy price volatility may raise input costs, mitigated by price variation clauses but not eliminated.

outlook.body:
- S1 — Deepen the core water franchise as a platform business, concentrating on bulk water transport from river to reservoir and high-ticket projects involving large-diameter pipelines, treatment infrastructure and integrated delivery; focus on fully-funded, state-backed projects with favourable payment terms, prefer pipeline-intensive, land-light contracts, and target selective geographies with proven administrative and payment track records.
- S2 — Selective expansion into BESS as a strategic adjacency through a manufacturing-and-technology-partnership model: establish the BESS manufacturing and integration facility in Pune, partner with Energy Vault for proprietary EMS software, and focus on containerised, modular solutions for grid, mobility and C&I segments — deliberately avoiding the capital intensity and chemistry risk of cell manufacturing.
- S3 — Quality of order book over quantity of orders: move away from a scale-chasing model, vet every bid for margin profile, fund-flow mechanism and execution complexity, bid only for projects with minimum 10% EBITDA potential, prioritise contracts with escrow-based payments or sovereign guarantees, and actively pursue recovery through arbitration and asset monetisation.
- S4 — Capital-light scaling via joint ventures and strategic partnerships: participate in large projects through commission-based JVs, earn fixed and performance-linked fees for project origination, design and oversight, and use existing pre-qualifications to enable larger bids without stretching the balance sheet.
- S5 — Drive execution efficiency through technology: deploy project control towers and cloud-based monitoring, standardise modular BESS designs for speed and quality, and automate billing and fund tracking.
- SPML 2.0 operating philosophy of selective bidding and margin discipline — remaining focused on fully-funded, high-margin, low-complexity projects rather than pursuing order-book expansion for its own sake.
- Treat FY2026-27 principally as a year of delivery: accelerate the renewed water and power EPC portfolio while maintaining commercial and working-capital discipline, and establish the BESS platform to utility-scale engineering, quality and safety standards.
- Build organisational capability ahead of the opportunity — strengthening project leadership and core execution functions while adding specialist expertise across battery systems, integration and technology, alongside project controls, procurement, safety, quality and risk management.
- Extend the role from asset creation into long-term operation, with several water projects carrying O&M periods of 10 to 20 years.
- Build an OEM revenue track alongside EPC — sizing the Pune facility beyond SPML's own pipeline to supply battery packs and containers directly to third-party EPC contractors.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: SPML's expansion in FY2025-26 is concentrated in the new Battery Energy Storage Systems vertical rather than in its asset-light water and power EPC core, where the BRSR records zero plants and twelve national offices. The Company is building a domestic BESS battery-pack and container assembly base at SUPA MIDC, Supa-Parner, Pune, developed in phases and supported by an exclusive technology tie-up with Energy Vault, USA for B-VAULT BESS technology and the VaultOS energy management software; the Board approved the phased development of a 5 GW BESS facility during the quarter ended 31st March 2025. The first phase of the 2.5 GWh assembly line is described as fully ready, with the MD&A stating the line is set to start by August 2026; the next phase of scale-up to 5 GWh alongside an annual manufacturing capacity of 600 container units is expected to complete in the first half of FY2027-28 (the MD&A and Outlook sections instead describe reaching 5 GWh and 600 containerised units 'by year-end', an internal inconsistency in the report). The facility is deliberately sized beyond SPML's own project pipeline so it can also supply battery packs and containers to third-party EPC contractors as an OEM. Certification is the gating step: battery-pack certification is underway at TUV China and expected to complete by August 2026, BESS certification testing with TUV India and TUV China is planned to commence from October 2026 after BESS integration at RCT China, and full absorption of the licensed technology is targeted after certification (target December 2026); Energy Vault will manufacture and supply two BESS units to Indian standards, one in China for certification and one at the Supa plant for internal integration and FAT. The Company is also securing IEC/UL certifications for its battery packs. Alongside the manufacturing build-out, the first utility-scale execution reference is the NTPC Barauni, Bihar BESS EPC order of approximately `1,128 crore covering 250 MW / 1,000 MWh with a 15-year O&M commitment, and the Company added a 400 kV grid substation and transmission project for RRPVNL at Kota, Rajasthan worth `165.4 crore. Funding flexibility for the BESS and container manufacturing facilities is stated to come from banking limits of `505 crore under enhancement plus `305 crore of surety bond limits, and the Directors' Report records a foreign currency outflow of `4,587.78 lakhs during FY2025-26 primarily towards pre-manufacturing expenses for establishing the new business plant. On the water side, expansion is contractual rather than capital: a renewed portfolio of Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0 and irrigation awards across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand and Bihar, several carrying O&M periods of 10 to 20 years.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Government's planned investment of approximately `17 lakh crore across flagship programmes such as Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0, Namami Gange and river-linking initiatives is expected to drive a robust pipeline of water supply and wastewater projects over the coming years.
- JJM 2.0 outlay enhanced to `8.69 lakh crore and extended to December 2028, backed by steady AMRUT 2.0 and state-level irrigation and inter-river-linking investments, offering a sustained pipeline for the water business.
- Union Budget FY27 allocated a record `12.2 lakh crore in capex with GDP growth projected at 6.6-6.9%, strengthening the outlook for a government-capex-driven EPC company.
- `1,09,029 crore allocated to the energy sector in FY27, driving investment in substations, grid modernisation and transmission — a core area of the Company's execution strength; RDSS adds `1.53 lakh crore for loss reduction and `1.31 lakh crore for smart metering.
- India's shift to a renewable-led, distributed generation mix (500 GW non-fossil target by 2030) makes storage a precondition rather than an adjacency; CEA estimates India will require over 236 GWh of BESS capacity by 2031-32.
- Indian BESS demand projected to grow from ~$2bn in 2026 to $8.6bn by 2031 at a CAGR of over 33%, with SPML building capacity ahead of the curve via the NTPC order and the Pune facility.
- Margin expansion is attributed to the SPML 2.0 operating model — disciplined project selection, asset-light execution and an increasing share of newer, better-priced contracts — with the Company expecting the FY26 margin trajectory to be further reinforced as execution shifts toward the new-project component of the order book.
- The Company expects healthy topline growth to continue into FY2026-27 and the following years, while prioritising profitability and execution discipline over pure revenue growth.
- BESS ramp-up, anchored by the NTPC order and the SUPA MIDC assembly facility, is expected to open a significant further avenue for growth as India's grid-scale storage requirement scales through the remainder of the decade.
- Improved credit profile (ICRA upgrade to BBB Stable, CRISIL assigned BBB Stable), enhanced lender credit limits of `505 crore and surety bond limits of `305 crore have strengthened liquidity to support both ongoing execution and future growth capex.
- Debt obligations of approximately `380 crore including interest over the next five years are expected to be comfortably met through arbitration proceeds of approximately `627 crore including interest accrued to March 2026.
- Focus on technically complex projects with high pre-qualification requirements, which management says enables improved execution quality, higher entry barriers and better profitability.
- Order book of approximately `5,369 crore as at 31st March 2026, up from `3,144 crore in FY2024-25 — an increase of approximately 71%.
- Approximately 75% of the year-end order book comprises new projects; around `4,000 crore is new, higher-margin work and `1,369 crore is legacy low-margin orders carried forward from earlier periods.
- The non-legacy portion consists predominantly of projects carrying expected operating margins of 10% or higher.
- New project orders worth approximately `5,600 crore were secured over the past year, independently or through joint ventures (Directors' Report).
- FY26 water and irrigation awards included Bharatpur, Rajasthan JJM at ~`1,438 crore (SPML share 51%, 10-year O&M); Indore AMRUT 2.0 at `1,073 crore (10-year O&M); Konar, Jharkhand irrigation at `618 crore benefiting 12,599 hectares (10-year O&M); Kekri-Sarwar (Package III), Ajmer, Rajasthan JJM at `385 crore (10-year O&M); Chennai AMRUT at `344.64 crore (SPML share 26%, 15-year O&M); Chennai reservoir/pumping/distribution at `258 crore (SPML share 26%, 20-year O&M); and Nonera, Jhalawar/Kota, Rajasthan JJM at `207 crore (SPML share 10%, 10-year O&M).
- April 2026 energy awards: NTPC Barauni, Bihar BESS EPC of approximately `1,128 crore — the largest single BESS order win to date — and a 400 kV grid substation and transmission project for RRPVNL at Kota, Rajasthan of `165.4 crore.
- Order book provides strong revenue visibility over the medium term, and pre-qualification credentials position the Company to secure large, complex water and energy projects.

risks.note: MD&A states a material part of revenue depends on the pace and scale of tenders floated by Government/municipal bodies under schemes such as Jal Jeevan Mission and AMRUT 2.0. This is structural: BRSR records EPC and O&M for Central and State Government infrastructure as 100% of turnover, with exports at 0%, so there is no non-government or overseas revenue to offset a slowdown in domestic scheme tendering.
risks.risk: Tender / order-inflow dependence on government schemes

risks.note: EPC contracts with government counterparties carry inherent risk of delayed collections and retention money release, notwithstanding mitigation through escrow mechanisms. The Chairman's message reinforces this, noting the renewed water portfolio requires working capital as execution gathers pace and that liquidity and cash conversion remain central to decisions; BRSR reports accounts payable days of 272 in FY2025-26 (267 in FY2024-25), including retention money.
risks.risk: Receivables and working-capital risk with government counterparties

risks.note: MD&A flags project delays arising from land acquisition, right-of-way, monsoon/seasonal factors and contractor/sub-contractor performance. The Chairman frames the same point commercially: an order is only the beginning of a commitment, and its real economics emerge through engineering, procurement, execution, billing and collection — the quality of the order book will be demonstrated through conversion.

Continued servicing of the NARCL settlement — a `700 crore total obligation over 8 years, of which `290 crore has been repaid — remains linked to the timing of awards-in-hand and expected recoveries on filed claims. MD&A separately states debt obligations of approximately `380 crore including interest over the next five years are expected to be met through arbitration proceeds of approximately `627 crore, so repayment capacity is contingent on recoveries the Company does not control.
risks.risk: Financial and leverage risk tied to the NARCL settlement

risks.note: The BESS segment is at a relatively early stage for the Company, carrying technology, supply-chain and demand-ramp-up risk associated with the Energy Vault collaboration and the planned manufacturing facility in Maharashtra. The segment remains in build-out and is only expected to be operational from 2026-2027, while the licensed technology is not yet fully absorbed and certification milestones are still ahead.
risks.risk: New-business risk in the BESS vertical

risks.note: Changes in government infrastructure policy, funding allocations (for example under JJM, AMRUT, or VGF for BESS) or energy storage obligation timelines could affect the pace of order inflow. MD&A separately flags that changes in environmental regulations, labour laws and other statutory requirements may increase compliance obligations and affect operational efficiency and cost structures.
risks.risk: Regulatory and policy risk on scheme funding

risks.note: MD&A flags ongoing legal and arbitration matters as disclosed elsewhere in the Annual Report and financial statements. This matters doubly because the Company also treats expected arbitration recoveries as the primary source of debt-repayment coverage, so adverse or delayed outcomes cut both ways.

MD&A states business selection and billing pace are tied to project fund availability, and any tightening at the client or agency level could affect revenue-recognition timelines; it cites the West Asia conflict, elevated crude prices and supply disruptions as having constrained fund availability and execution pace in March FY26. Commodity and energy price volatility may raise input costs, mitigated by price variation clauses but not eliminated.
risks.risk: Execution pace tied to client-side fund availability, and commodity/geopolitical cost exposure

The Company is building a domestic BESS battery-pack and container assembly base at SUPA MIDC, Supa-Parner, Pune, developed in phases and supported by an exclusive technology tie-up with Energy Vault, USA for B-VAULT BESS technology and the VaultOS energy management software; the Board approved the phased development of a 5 GW BESS facility during the quarter ended 31st March 2025. The first phase of the 2.5 GWh assembly line is described as fully ready, with the MD&A stating the line is set to start by August 2026; the next phase of scale-up to 5 GWh alongside an annual manufacturing capacity of 600 container units is expected to complete in the first half of FY2027-28 (the MD&A and Outlook sections instead describe reaching 5 GWh and 600 containerised units 'by year-end', an internal inconsistency in the report). The facility is deliberately sized beyond SPML's own project pipeline so it can also supply battery packs and containers to third-party EPC contractors as an OEM. Certification is the gating step: battery-pack certification is underway at TUV China and expected to complete by August 2026, BESS certification testing with TUV India and TUV China is planned to commence from October 2026 after BESS integration at RCT China, and full absorption of the licensed technology is targeted after certification (target December 2026); Energy Vault will manufacture and supply two BESS units to Indian standards, one in China for certification and one at the Supa plant for internal integration and FAT. The Company is also securing IEC/UL certifications for its battery packs. Alongside the manufacturing build-out, the first utility-scale execution reference is the NTPC Barauni, Bihar BESS EPC order of approximately `1,128 crore covering 250 MW / 1,000 MWh with a 15-year O&M commitment, and the Company added a 400 kV grid substation and transmission project for RRPVNL at Kota, Rajasthan worth `165.4 crore. Funding flexibility for the BESS and container manufacturing facilities is stated to come from banking limits of `505 crore under enhancement plus `305 crore of surety bond limits, and the Directors' Report records a foreign currency outflow of `4,587.78 lakhs during FY2025-26 primarily towards pre-manufacturing expenses for establishing the new business plant. On the water side, expansion is contractual rather than capital: a renewed portfolio of Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0 and irrigation awards across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand and Bihar, several carrying O&M periods of 10 to 20 years.

risks.risk: Tender / order-inflow dependence on government schemes
risks.note: MD&A states a material part of revenue depends on the pace and scale of tenders floated by Government/municipal bodies under schemes such as Jal Jeevan Mission and AMRUT 2.0. This is structural: BRSR records EPC and O&M for Central and State Government infrastructure as 100% of turnover, with exports at 0%, so there is no non-government or overseas revenue to offset a slowdown in domestic scheme tendering.

risks.risk: Receivables and working-capital risk with government counterparties
risks.note: EPC contracts with government counterparties carry inherent risk of delayed collections and retention money release, notwithstanding mitigation through escrow mechanisms. The Chairman's message reinforces this, noting the renewed water portfolio requires working capital as execution gathers pace and that liquidity and cash conversion remain central to decisions; BRSR reports accounts payable days of 272 in FY2025-26 (267 in FY2024-25), including retention money.

MD&A flags project delays arising from land acquisition, right-of-way, monsoon/seasonal factors and contractor/sub-contractor performance. The Chairman frames the same point commercially: an order is only the beginning of a commitment, and its real economics emerge through engineering, procurement, execution, billing and collection — the quality of the order book will be demonstrated through conversion.

risks.risk: Financial and leverage risk tied to the NARCL settlement
risks.note: Continued servicing of the NARCL settlement — a `700 crore total obligation over 8 years, of which `290 crore has been repaid — remains linked to the timing of awards-in-hand and expected recoveries on filed claims. MD&A separately states debt obligations of approximately `380 crore including interest over the next five years are expected to be met through arbitration proceeds of approximately `627 crore, so repayment capacity is contingent on recoveries the Company does not control.

risks.risk: New-business risk in the BESS vertical
risks.note: The BESS segment is at a relatively early stage for the Company, carrying technology, supply-chain and demand-ramp-up risk associated with the Energy Vault collaboration and the planned manufacturing facility in Maharashtra. The segment remains in build-out and is only expected to be operational from 2026-2027, while the licensed technology is not yet fully absorbed and certification milestones are still ahead.

risks.risk: Regulatory and policy risk on scheme funding
risks.note: Changes in government infrastructure policy, funding allocations (for example under JJM, AMRUT, or VGF for BESS) or energy storage obligation timelines could affect the pace of order inflow. MD&A separately flags that changes in environmental regulations, labour laws and other statutory requirements may increase compliance obligations and affect operational efficiency and cost structures.

MD&A flags ongoing legal and arbitration matters as disclosed elsewhere in the Annual Report and financial statements. This matters doubly because the Company also treats expected arbitration recoveries as the primary source of debt-repayment coverage, so adverse or delayed outcomes cut both ways.

risks.risk: Execution pace tied to client-side fund availability, and commodity/geopolitical cost exposure
risks.note: MD&A states business selection and billing pace are tied to project fund availability, and any tightening at the client or agency level could affect revenue-recognition timelines; it cites the West Asia conflict, elevated crude prices and supply disruptions as having constrained fund availability and execution pace in March FY26. Commodity and energy price volatility may raise input costs, mitigated by price variation clauses but not eliminated.

one-line thesis: Post-NARCL-resolution water EPC executing a clean SPML 2.0 reset — selective ≥10%-margin new orders, legacy back-to-back book running off, and an optionality leg in BESS manufacturing (Energy Vault tie-up, NTPC ₹1,128 cr win) — with arbitration awards (not cash flow) earmarked to extinguish residual NARCL dues, making it "effectively debt-free."
financial scorecard:

- **Revenue:** ₹293.9 cr, +53% YoY, +27% QoQ.
- **EBITDA:** ₹25 cr, margin 8.4% (reported). Depressed by one-offs: legal/consultancy costs on arbitration matter; non-cash ECL provision (Ind AS); bank-limit mobilization costs (~₹10 cr aggregate increase in other expenditure). Normalized margin ~10% per mgmt.
- **PAT:** ₹28 cr, +140% YoY. Aided by tax reversal (recognition of tax benefit on accumulated income-tax losses) and write-back of operating liabilities booked under other income.

**FY26 (full year, consolidated):**
- **Revenue:** ₹868 cr, +13% YoY (mgmt also cites "~₹887 cr"; guidance was ₹900–1,000 cr → shortfall, see §3).
- **EBITDA:** ₹86 cr, +37% YoY; margin 9.7%.
- **PAT:** ₹76 cr, +55% YoY.

**Order book:** Consolidated OB ₹5,369 cr entering Q4 (~₹4,000 cr new + ₹1,369 cr legacy); inflection-point figure also cited as ₹5,368 cr / ₹5,616 cr (incl. ~₹1,300 cr power inc. BESS + substation). Net-of-consortium water OB ≈ ₹3,300 cr. New orders ≥₹4,280 cr (incl. JV share) secured since FY25.

**Net debt / deleveraging [KEY]:**
- D/E rose to 0.4x; Net debt/EBITDA 4.41x; ROE 8%.
- **NARCL:** total outstanding incl. interest ₹380 cr as on 31-Mar-26 vs agreed ₹700 cr. Cumulative paid over 3 yrs ₹319–320 cr vs agreed ₹271 cr (i.e. prepaid ahead of schedule; ₹47–48 cr prepayment against FY27-28 dues).
- **Arbitration:** ₹312–315 cr awards received since resolution; ~₹627–630 cr awards in hand (advanced/Supreme-Court stage); ~₹4,500 cr additional claims pending (~40% historical conversion → ~₹1,500 cr expected). ~75% of award proceeds routed to NARCL. Mgmt: "effectively a debt-free company" on a cash-flow basis — surplus cash reserved for growth, not NARCL.
- **Liquidity:** ₹476 cr raised since May-2024 (promoter contribution ₹313.5 cr, over and above ₹112.5 cr in the difficult period). Bank credit limit enhanced to ₹505 cr; surety-bond exposure ₹305 cr (in lieu of BG, low margin).

**Working capital:** Trade receivables up ₹299.55 cr → ₹417.50 cr; of which ₹137 cr back-to-back (matched creditor liability, no WC blocked), ₹186 cr "normal" debtors (realize in normal cycle), balance retention/others. Creditors rose in tandem (escrow mechanism — debtors covered by creditors, company fund minimally used). Other current assets up on Ind AS inventory provision.
guidance (critical):
- **Revenue:** ">25% growth in FY27" at both top line AND bottom line; growth momentum to continue subsequent years. Quarter-on-quarter increase expected each quarter. ~₹50–100 cr of FY26 execution shortfall spills into FY27 (mostly Q1/Q2).
- **Margin:** EBITDA target ~10%; expected to rise as new-order mix increases (all new orders ≥10%, legacy small-but-protected). Detailed FY27/FY28 split deferred — yearly guidance to be given at each annual call.

margins & cost dynamics:
- Target ≥10% EBITDA on all new business (hard floor — "less than 10%, we don't do any business"). FY26 reported EBITDA margin 9.7%; Q4 8.4% optically low on one-offs.
- Margin lift mechanism: rising share of new (higher-margin, price-protected) orders vs legacy low-margin JV; all new orders carry PV (price-variation) clause → escalation/crude-price protection.
- Labor: already accruing per new Labor Code, no cost shock; labor availability not an issue.

capex / expansion (watch slippage):

- 2.5 GW line commences end-Jun-2026; 5 GW + 600 containers by end-FY27 — **slippage watch:** dates are near-term and BESS execution is new to the company.
- Funded by ₹476 cr raised since May-2024 (incl. promoter ₹313.5 cr) — used for BESS capex, container facility and project working capital.
capital allocation (deleveraging — centr:
- NARCL residual ₹380 cr (vs ₹700 cr agreed), prepaying ahead of schedule; minimum ₹45 cr more in FY27 to neutralize FY27-28 liability; then attack FY28-29.
- Deleveraging funded ~entirely by arbitration award monetization (~75% of proceeds → NARCL), NOT operating cash flow → operating surplus freed for growth (BESS capex, WC).
- Equity raised ₹476 cr (promoter-heavy) demonstrates skin-in-the-game; bank limit ₹505 cr; surety bonds ₹305 cr to economize on BG/margin.
- No dividend discussed. Tax shield: accumulated losses >₹500 cr + new tax regime (no MAT) → minimal cash tax for "a few years."
risks & watch-items:
- **Arbitration dependency:** Entire deleveraging thesis hinges on timely arbitration realizations (~40% claim-to-award conversion assumed; some at Supreme Court — timing/quantum uncertain).
- **Legacy NARCL dues** still ₹380 cr on books despite "effectively debt-free" framing.
- **Working capital / receivables:** receivables jumped to ₹417.5 cr; reliance on escrow/back-to-back netting; govt-payment cycle risk (esp. PHED/state water vs NTPC/PowerGrid which pay in 15–30 days).
- **Jal Jeevan payment risk:** mgmt acknowledges JJM payments were stopped for verification (now resuming); SPML avoided JJM during stress, only re-entering selectively.
- **Funding-paced execution:** revenue calibrated to customer fund availability → top-line lumpiness (FY26 miss); West-Asia-war crude/supply headwinds (mitigated by PV clauses).
- **BESS execution risk:** new manufacturing vertical, ambitious capacity ramp, oversupply concern (mgmt downplays via Energy Vault tie-up + 30-40 yr power EPC pedigree).
- **One-off-reliant Q4 PAT** (tax reversal + liability write-back) — quality of earnings.
management quality / tone: Confident, detailed, candid on the FY26 turnover miss (owned it, explained funding discipline). Repeatedly stresses "SPML 2.0" discipline — quality over volume, ≥10% margin floor, PV clause, fully-funded orders only. CFO Manoj Digga dominated; technical BESS depth from Malay Chakraborti. Framing of "effectively debt-free" is optimistic and should be read against ₹380 cr residual NARCL + arbitration-timing risk. Promoter has injected meaningful equity — alignment positive.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The real deleveraging engine is the litigation book (~₹4,500 cr claims), not EBITDA — SPML is partly an arbitration-recovery story dressed as an EPC.
- "Order book met, turnover missed" — for an EPC the order book is the leading indicator; FY26 shortfall is a timing (funding-paced) issue that converts to FY27-28 revenue, not a demand loss.
- BESS is genuinely differentiated optionality (only Indian player with Energy Vault tie-up + own battery-pack/container manufacturing) but is capacity/execution unproven — a 5 GW line implies ~₹5,000 cr revenue potential vs ₹868 cr current total.
- Margin trajectory is structurally up purely on mix shift (legacy run-off → new ≥10% orders) even before BESS scales.
- Back-to-back legacy contracts inflate gross receivables/payables but are cash-flow-neutral — headline WC looks worse than economic reality.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: SPML Infra is a four-decade-old Indian EPC contractor for water infrastructure that has extended into power T&D and, from FY2025-26, utility-scale battery energy storage, closing the year with an order book of `5,369 crore.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Incorporated in 1981, SPML Infra designs, procures, builds, commissions and increasingly operates water and energy infrastructure for Central and State Government and municipal clients under EPC, PPP and BOOT models. Its water franchise spans source development, intake, treatment, pumping, bulk transmission, storage, irrigation, urban and rural distribution, metering, wastewater and reuse, while its energy business covers substations, transmission, distribution and rural electrification and, newly, utility-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems. Several water contracts carry operations and maintenance periods of 10 to 20 years, so responsibility extends well beyond commissioning.

- **BESS (key optionality):** 2.5 GW assembly line at Supa MIDC Pune commencing ~end-Jun-2026; expand to 5 GW + 600 containerized BESS units/yr by end-FY27. Peak revenue potential ~₹2,500 cr (2.5 GW) → ~₹5,000 cr (5 GW). Three models — EPC (~10%), OEM battery-pack supply to other EPCs (~10%, 3–6 month turnaround), O&M. India BESS TAM cited 236 GW by 2031-32; market ~$2 bn (2026) → $8.6 bn (2031), ~33% CAGR; 10% BESS mandate on renewables.
- **River-linking / irrigation:** Ken-Betwa, PKC, Wainganga-Nalganga — focus optionality for FY27-28.
- **Power T&D / substations:** leading player; rising govt focus (Union Budget energy allocation ₹1,09,029 cr).
- **Long-term mix goal:** water ~50% / power+BESS ~50% by FY30 (from current 75:25 → balancing).

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Government's planned investment of approximately `17 lakh crore across flagship programmes such as Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0, Namami Gange and river-linking initiatives is expected to drive a robust pipeline of water supply and wastewater projects over the coming years.
- JJM 2.0 outlay enhanced to `8.69 lakh crore and extended to December 2028, backed by steady AMRUT 2.0 and state-level irrigation and inter-river-linking investments, offering a sustained pipeline for the water business.
- Union Budget FY27 allocated a record `12.2 lakh crore in capex with GDP growth projected at 6.6-6.9%, strengthening the outlook for a government-capex-driven EPC company.
- `1,09,029 crore allocated to the energy sector in FY27, driving investment in substations, grid modernisation and transmission — a core area of the Company's execution strength; RDSS adds `1.53 lakh crore for loss reduction and `1.31 lakh crore for smart metering.
- India's shift to a renewable-led, distributed generation mix (500 GW non-fossil target by 2030) makes storage a precondition rather than an adjacency; CEA estimates India will require over 236 GWh of BESS capacity by 2031-32.
- Indian BESS demand projected to grow from ~$2bn in 2026 to $8.6bn by 2031 at a CAGR of over 33%, with SPML building capacity ahead of the curve via the NTPC order and the Pune facility.
- Margin expansion is attributed to the SPML 2.0 operating model — disciplined project selection, asset-light execution and an increasing share of newer, better-priced contracts — with the Company expecting the FY26 margin trajectory to be further reinforced as execution shifts toward the new-project component of the order book.
- The Company expects healthy topline growth to continue into FY2026-27 and the following years, while prioritising profitability and execution discipline over pure revenue growth.
- BESS ramp-up, anchored by the NTPC order and the SUPA MIDC assembly facility, is expected to open a significant further avenue for growth as India's grid-scale storage requirement scales through the remainder of the decade.
- Improved credit profile (ICRA upgrade to BBB Stable, CRISIL assigned BBB Stable), enhanced lender credit limits of `505 crore and surety bond limits of `305 crore have strengthened liquidity to support both ongoing execution and future growth capex.
- Debt obligations of approximately `380 crore including interest over the next five years are expected to be comfortably met through arbitration proceeds of approximately `627 crore including interest accrued to March 2026.
- Focus on technically complex projects with high pre-qualification requirements, which management says enables improved execution quality, higher entry barriers and better profitability.
- Order book of approximately `5,369 crore as at 31st March 2026, up from `3,144 crore in FY2024-25 — an increase of approximately 71%.
- Approximately 75% of the year-end order book comprises new projects; around `4,000 crore is new, higher-margin work and `1,369 crore is legacy low-margin orders carried forward from earlier periods.
- The non-legacy portion consists predominantly of projects carrying expected operating margins of 10% or higher.
- New project orders worth approximately `5,600 crore were secured over the past year, independently or through joint ventures (Directors' Report).
- FY26 water and irrigation awards included Bharatpur, Rajasthan JJM at ~`1,438 crore (SPML share 51%, 10-year O&M); Indore AMRUT 2.0 at `1,073 crore (10-year O&M); Konar, Jharkhand irrigation at `618 crore benefiting 12,599 hectares (10-year O&M); Kekri-Sarwar (Package III), Ajmer, Rajasthan JJM at `385 crore (10-year O&M); Chennai AMRUT at `344.64 crore (SPML share 26%, 15-year O&M); Chennai reservoir/pumping/distribution at `258 crore (SPML share 26%, 20-year O&M); and Nonera, Jhalawar/Kota, Rajasthan JJM at `207 crore (SPML share 10%, 10-year O&M).
- April 2026 energy awards: NTPC Barauni, Bihar BESS EPC of approximately `1,128 crore — the largest single BESS order win to date — and a 400 kV grid substation and transmission project for RRPVNL at Kota, Rajasthan of `165.4 crore.
- Order book provides strong revenue visibility over the medium term, and pre-qualification credentials position the Company to secure large, complex water and energy projects.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body:
- Target ≥10% EBITDA on all new business (hard floor — "less than 10%, we don't do any business"). FY26 reported EBITDA margin 9.7%; Q4 8.4% optically low on one-offs.
- Margin lift mechanism: rising share of new (higher-margin, price-protected) orders vs legacy low-margin JV; all new orders carry PV (price-variation) clause → escalation/crude-price protection.
- Labor: already accruing per new Labor Code, no cost shock; labor availability not an issue.
- BESS margins: EPC and OEM both ~10%; OEM faster turnaround.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation (deleveraging — central)
capital_allocation.body:
- NARCL residual ₹380 cr (vs ₹700 cr agreed), prepaying ahead of schedule; minimum ₹45 cr more in FY27 to neutralize FY27-28 liability; then attack FY28-29.
- Deleveraging funded ~entirely by arbitration award monetization (~75% of proceeds → NARCL), NOT operating cash flow → operating surplus freed for growth (BESS capex, WC).
- Equity raised ₹476 cr (promoter-heavy) demonstrates skin-in-the-game; bank limit ₹505 cr; surety bonds ₹305 cr to economize on BG/margin.
- No dividend discussed. Tax shield: accumulated losses >₹500 cr + new tax regime (no MAT) → minimal cash tax for "a few years."

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: SPML's expansion in FY2025-26 is concentrated in the new Battery Energy Storage Systems vertical rather than in its asset-light water and power EPC core, where the BRSR records zero plants and twelve national offices. The Company is building a domestic BESS battery-pack and container assembly base at SUPA MIDC, Supa-Parner, Pune, developed in phases and supported by an exclusive technology tie-up with Energy Vault, USA for B-VAULT BESS technology and the VaultOS energy management software; the Board approved the phased development of a 5 GW BESS facility during the quarter ended 31st March 2025. The first phase of the 2.5 GWh assembly line is described as fully ready, with the MD&A stating the line is set to start by August 2026; the next phase of scale-up to 5 GWh alongside an annual manufacturing capacity of 600 container units is expected to complete in the first half of FY2027-28 (the MD&A and Outlook sections instead describe reaching 5 GWh and 600 containerised units 'by year-end', an internal inconsistency in the report). The facility is deliberately sized beyond SPML's own project pipeline so it can also supply battery packs and containers to third-party EPC contractors as an OEM. Certification is the gating step: battery-pack certification is underway at TUV China and expected to complete by August 2026, BESS certification testing with TUV India and TUV China is planned to commence from October 2026 after BESS integration at RCT China, and full absorption of the licensed technology is targeted after certification (target December 2026); Energy Vault will manufacture and supply two BESS units to Indian standards, one in China for certification and one at the Supa plant for internal integration and FAT. The Company is also securing IEC/UL certifications for its battery packs. Alongside the manufacturing build-out, the first utility-scale execution reference is the NTPC Barauni, Bihar BESS EPC order of approximately `1,128 crore covering 250 MW / 1,000 MWh with a 15-year O&M commitment, and the Company added a 400 kV grid substation and transmission project for RRPVNL at Kota, Rajasthan worth `165.4 crore. Funding flexibility for the BESS and container manufacturing facilities is stated to come from banking limits of `505 crore under enhancement plus `305 crore of surety bond limits, and the Directors' Report records a foreign currency outflow of `4,587.78 lakhs during FY2025-26 primarily towards pre-manufacturing expenses for establishing the new business plant. On the water side, expansion is contractual rather than capital: a renewed portfolio of Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0 and irrigation awards across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand and Bihar, several carrying O&M periods of 10 to 20 years.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Over four decades and 700+ executed projects give high pre-qualification credentials, which the Company states create higher entry barriers and better profitability on technically complex work
- Integrated in-house delivery framework spanning design and engineering, procurement, project management, construction, erection, testing and commissioning
- Deep water reference base: 10,000+ km of pipelines, infrastructure serving 50 million+ people, and treatment assets including the 200 MLD Surajpura, 160 MLD Dhannaser, 125 MLD Pokhran, 100 MLD Goa and 68 MLD Hubli-Dharwad WTPs
- Long-duration O&M attached to several water projects (10 to 20 years) converts one-off EPC delivery into recurring lifecycle responsibility and revenue
- Power heritage — 100+ substation projects from 33 kV to 400 kV, GIS substations, APDRP work covering 70 substations and electrification of 20,000+ villages — provides the grid-interface capability BESS requires
- Exclusive tie-up with Energy Vault (US) for B-VAULT technology and VaultOS EMS, described as making SPML the first Indian company with this BESS technology, allowing entry into storage without recreating the technology stack or taking cell-chemistry risk
- Strengthened balance sheet and improved credit profile: ICRA upgraded the rating to BBB (Stable) and CRISIL assigned BBB (Stable), supporting access to funding and larger bids

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Arbitration dependency:** Entire deleveraging thesis hinges on timely arbitration realizations (~40% claim-to-award conversion assumed; some at Supreme Court — timing/quantum uncertain).
- **Legacy NARCL dues** still ₹380 cr on books despite "effectively debt-free" framing.
- **Working capital / receivables:** receivables jumped to ₹417.5 cr; reliance on escrow/back-to-back netting; govt-payment cycle risk (esp. PHED/state water vs NTPC/PowerGrid which pay in 15–30 days).
- **Jal Jeevan payment risk:** mgmt acknowledges JJM payments were stopped for verification (now resuming); SPML avoided JJM during stress, only re-entering selectively.
- **Funding-paced execution:** revenue calibrated to customer fund availability → top-line lumpiness (FY26 miss); West-Asia-war crude/supply headwinds (mitigated by PV clauses).
- **BESS execution risk:** new manufacturing vertical, ambitious capacity ramp, oversupply concern (mgmt downplays via Energy Vault tie-up + 30-40 yr power EPC pedigree).
- **One-off-reliant Q4 PAT** (tax reversal + liability write-back) — quality of earnings.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The real deleveraging engine is the litigation book (~₹4,500 cr claims), not EBITDA — SPML is partly an arbitration-recovery story dressed as an EPC.
- "Order book met, turnover missed" — for an EPC the order book is the leading indicator; FY26 shortfall is a timing (funding-paced) issue that converts to FY27-28 revenue, not a demand loss.
- BESS is genuinely differentiated optionality (only Indian player with Energy Vault tie-up + own battery-pack/container manufacturing) but is capacity/execution unproven — a 5 GW line implies ~₹5,000 cr revenue potential vs ₹868 cr current total.
- Margin trajectory is structurally up purely on mix shift (legacy run-off → new ≥10% orders) even before BESS scales.
- Back-to-back legacy contracts inflate gross receivables/payables but are cash-flow-neutral — headline WC looks worse than economic reality.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- S1 — Deepen the core water franchise as a platform business, concentrating on bulk water transport from river to reservoir and high-ticket projects involving large-diameter pipelines, treatment infrastructure and integrated delivery; focus on fully-funded, state-backed projects with favourable payment terms, prefer pipeline-intensive, land-light contracts, and target selective geographies with proven administrative and payment track records.
- S2 — Selective expansion into BESS as a strategic adjacency through a manufacturing-and-technology-partnership model: establish the BESS manufacturing …

themes.need: AMRUT, Namami Gange and Jal Jeevan still define the pipeline, but Q1FY27 put a number on the funding freeze. WPIL's consolidated revenue rose 32% to INR 501cr while STANDALONE collapsed 37% to INR 115cr as domestic Jal Jeevan invoicing froze, with INR 300-350cr of JJM receivables pending (mostly West Bengal, some MP) and nil received in the quarter - management expects substantial inflow only in Q2/H2.
